name: Train and Peter
description: During a train trip from city A to B, Peter wakes up twice. He records two non-overlapping, chronological sequences of flag colors he sees at stations. Given the complete sequence of flags from A to B and Peter's two recorded sequences, determine if his observations are possible on the forward trip (A->B), the backward trip (B->A, which is the A->B sequence reversed), both, or neither.

input_spec.line_1: String: The full sequence of flag colors from A to B.
input_spec.line_2: String: The first sequence Peter observed.
input_spec.line_3: String: The second sequence Peter observed.

output_spec.description: Output a single word indicating the validity of Peter's story:

options.forward: Possible only on the A to B trip.
options.backward: Possible only on the B to A trip.

examples.title: Problem Example 1: Simple Forward Case
examples.why_included: This is the first example from the problem statement, testing the most basic 'forward' scenario.

examples.title: Problem Example 2: Simple Both Case on Palindrome
examples.why_included: This is the second example from the problem statement, testing a 'both' scenario where the main string is a palindrome.

examples.title: Simple Backward Case
examples.why_included: A minimal, non-palindromic string where the sequences only appear in the correct order on the backward journey.

examples.title: Simple Fantasy Case with Missing Substrings
examples.why_included: A basic case where neither of the two required sequences are present in the main string.

examples.title: Fantasy Case: Substrings Present in Wrong Order
examples.why_included: Tests that the first sequence must appear chronologically before the second. Both substrings are present, but not in the required order.

examples.title: Both Case on a Non-Palindromic String
examples.why_included: Demonstrates a 'both' result on a non-palindromic string, requiring checks on both the original and its reverse.

examples.title: Identical Subsequences, Adjacent
examples.why_included: Tests when the two required sequences are identical and appear back-to-back, requiring careful indexing in the search.

examples.title: Identical Subsequences, Insufficient Space
examples.why_included: Tests an edge case where a match for the first sequence is found, but there's not enough remaining string for the second identical sequence.

examples.title: Minimal Forward Case
examples.why_included: The smallest possible input that results in 'forward'.

examples.title: Minimal Both Case
examples.why_included: The smallest possible input that results in 'both', using a palindrome.

examples.title: Minimal Backward Case
examples.why_included: The smallest possible input that results in 'backward'.

examples.title: Minimal Fantasy Case
examples.why_included: The smallest possible input that results in 'fantasy'.

examples.title: Greedy First Match is Correct
examples.why_included: This case confirms that finding the first occurrence of the first substring and then searching is the correct strategy. There are multiple 'abra's.

examples.title: Fantasy due to Overlapping Substrings
examples.why_included: Tests that the second substring must begin strictly after the first one ends. A naive find might succeed, but chronological order makes it impossible.

examples.title: Main String of All Same Characters
examples.why_included: Tests a simple case on a monotonous string. It works in both directions because the string is a palindrome.

examples.title: All Same Characters, Fantasy
examples.why_included: Tests a case where there isn't enough space for two non-overlapping instances of the same substring.

examples.title: Forward OK, Backward has Patterns in Wrong Order
examples.why_included: A constructed case where both patterns are present in both directions, but only in the correct chronological order in the forward direction.

examples.title: One Pattern is a Prefix of the Other
examples.why_included: Tests edge case where one search pattern is a prefix of the other, which could confuse naive implementations.

examples.title: First Substring Not Found
examples.why_included: Tests the case where the second substring is present but the first is not, which must result in fantasy.

examples.title: Second Substring Not Found
examples.why_included: Tests the case where the first substring is present but the second is not, which must result in fantasy.

examples.title: Full String is the Concatenation of Patterns
examples.why_included: A simple case where the main string is just the two patterns joined together.

examples.title: Max Length Patterns at Opposite Ends of Max Length String
examples.why_included: This is constructed from P1, a long gap of 'c's, and P2. The gap prevents finding P2 after P1. The key is that the input strings are different. P1 is at the start of S, but the required P2 is not present at all. It tests performance on max-length inputs. The provided input has S=a...ab...b, P1=a...a, P2=b...b. Forward fails because P2 does not come after P1. Backward fails because the order is wrong.

examples.title: Max Length Patterns, Touching in Max Length String
examples.why_included: Tests performance with max-length inputs where the patterns are adjacent and embedded within a much larger string.

examples.title: Stress Test with Long Repeated Patterns
examples.why_included: Uses highly repetitive, periodic strings. This is a pathological case for naive string searching algorithms and tests the efficiency of the underlying implementation (e.g., KMP, Boyer-Moore).

examples.title: Large Random String, Forward Case
examples.why_included: A general test case with random characters surrounding the two patterns to ensure they can be found in a noisy environment. Seed: 123.

examples.title: Large Random String, Backward Case
examples.why_included: A general test case with random characters where the patterns appear in the correct chronological order only on the backward trip. Seed: 456.

examples.title: Large Random String, Both Case
examples.why_included: A palindromic string constructed with random-like parts, ensuring the condition holds for both forward and backward directions. Seed: 789.

examples.title: Large Random String, Fantasy Case
examples.why_included: A general test case with random characters where the patterns do not appear in the correct chronological order in either direction. Seed: 1337.

examples.title: Forward OK, Backward has Patterns in Wrong Order
examples.why_included: A constructed case where both patterns are present in both directions, but only in the correct chronological order in the forward direction. The reversed string contains 'piper' before 'peter'.

examples.title: Palindromic Patterns Creating Forward-Only Case
examples.why_included: Tests a case where both patterns are palindromes. In the reversed string, 'radar' appears before 'level', making the backward journey impossible, isolating the 'forward' result.

examples.title: Overlapping Search Patterns Test
examples.why_included: Tests the search logic with overlapping patterns. The first 'aba' (index 0) is found, and 'ba' is correctly found after it (index 3). The main string is a palindrome, so it works both ways.

examples.title: Complex Palindrome Resulting in 'Both'
examples.why_included: A non-trivial palindromic string where the patterns can be found correctly in both directions, confirming the symmetry of the checking logic.

examples.title: One Pattern is a Substring of the Other
examples.why_included: Tests a tricky case where one pattern is a substring of the other. The first pattern is found, but the second does not appear *after* it, leading to a 'fantasy' result.

examples.title: Constructed Tricky Backward-Only Case
examples.why_included: This string is the reverse of 'one_gap_two'. The forward search fails, but the backward search (on the reversed string) finds 'one' then 'two' in the correct order.
